title: "It doesn't learn": an architecture for a learning loop in AI agents
description: Agent memory from user corrections: why 'store and inject' fails, and a seven-stage loop with provenance, a taxonomy, budgets, replay evals and human gates.
summary: Users say their AI assistant does not learn: they correct it on Monday, and on Tuesday it makes the same mistake. The model is not the problem; it is stateless by design. The system around it never records what the user said in a checkable way, never sorts those notes into kinds, and never tests whether they help. This article lays out a loop that does all three: record, enrich, group, extract, serve, evaluate, approve. A person signs off at every stage. It also says when a simpler option is enough, and includes a small runnable example.

keyTerms.definition: A pipeline that turns past interactions into checked, typed notes, serves a small set of them to future sessions, and measures whether answers improved before anything goes live.

One immutable entry per user turn holding the question, the answer the user actually saw, the feedback, provenance such as ids and timestamps, and the id of the package that was in context. Every later file is derived from it.
A single extracted note with a kind (world fact, method rule, answer shape, profile or watch), a scope, a verbatim quote from the user and a pointer to the record it came from.

The budgeted, layered text served to a new session: rules first, world facts in 'verify then apply' form, and a list of anything cut or superseded. Each package has a manifest and a live pointer per user.
Answering old questions again with and without the package, then scoring the two answers with a blind judge, code guards and the user's own later corrections.
Writing the hypothesis, pass line, sample and judge prompt before a run, and pinning code and prompt hashes so results cannot quietly reshape the test.
An appended event that withdraws a user's words. Views are rebuilt from the log plus the tombstone, so the quote disappears everywhere without editing any record.

keyPoints: "It doesn't learn" is a design problem in the system around the model: stateless model, stateful system.
Storing corrections and injecting them fails because kinds get mixed, facts go stale, text leaks, lists grow and nothing is measured.
Parse each interaction once into an immutable record with provenance and the package id that was in context; everything else is a rebuildable view.
Give every learning a kind, a scope and an owner; per-user beats shared, specific beats general, newer beats older, in that order.
Every served item must quote the user's own words, checked by code against the record; world facts are served as dated claims to verify, never as statements.
Budget the package, render it in layers, list what was cut or superseded, and place it in the stable prefix after the system text.
Evaluate by replay against what the user later corrected, with a pointwise or pairwise judge chosen deliberately, and pre-register the pass line before the run.
Keep one human gate per stage; 'live' is a pointer per user, so rollback moves the pointer and never edits.
Build the loop only when corrections are per-user, recur across sessions and someone is accountable for a wrong answer; otherwise notes, retrieval or a vendor memory tool may be enough.
videoOutline: Hook (Short): Your AI assistant should never remember a fact. It should remember that you said it, on a date, and that it needs checking.
The complaint: corrected on Monday, repeated on Tuesday. The model is stateless by design; the system around it is what forgets.
The obvious fix: store corrections, inject them next time, and the five ways it breaks within a month.
The mental model: seven stages, record to approve, drawn as a loop, with a file on every arrow and a person at every gate.
Story: an older pipeline where learned claims were injected into every stage with no cap, and cost rose without bound. Budget from day one.
Record and structure: one immutable record per turn, sidecars for enrichment, the taxonomy of five kinds, and humans freezing the vocabulary.
Extract and serve: verbatim quotes checked by code, 'verify then apply' for world facts, budgets, layers, listed cuts, and where the package sits in the prompt.
Prove it: replay with and without the package, pointwise versus pairwise judges, scoring against the user's later corrections, pre-registration and pinned hashes.
Demo: run the script. One item rejected for a paraphrase, one for a bare fact, the package with a listed cut and a superseded item, both arms scored, one leak flag, the pinned hash.
Keep it running: one gate per stage, the package manifest, 'live' as a pointer, rollback without edits, and withdrawal by tombstone.
When this loop is the wrong tool: notes, vendor memory, retrieval and fine-tuning compared, and the rule of thumb for building it.
Close: the day 1 and week 1 checklist, and the line to remember. Approval is a step, not a hope.
